newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Foreign states involved in Afghan war, says U.N..
newsitem.headline: Foreign states involved in Afghan war, says U.N..

text.p: Senior U.N. official Marrack Goulding, seeking to secure peace in Afghanistan, said on Saturday a number of foreign countries were involved in the conflict but declined to name them.
The Under-Secretary for Political Affairs spoke at a news conference after two days of talks with the embattled government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Goulding said the problem in implementing a peace formula was a lack of willingness by parties to engage in serious political talks.
He said the latest fighting "does not show that (the rebel group) Taleban have given up military options". The Islamic militia now controls more than half of Afghanistan.

"I think it is a common knowledge that a number of countries are playing a part in the conflict," Goulding said when asked about Kabul's charge that neighbouring Pakistan was helping Taleban, which has captured two eastern provinces in the past week.

He said the matter had been discussed with the Pakistan ambassador at the United Nations, but added: "I don't want to raise a finger at any particular member state though I can confirm that a number of states are involved."
Pakistan denies aiding Taleban and says it has no favourites among the warring Afghan factions, most of whom it helped during their war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
Rabbani's military commander Ahmad Shah Masood told Goulding that peace would not return to Afghanistan as long as Pakistan continued to interfere, a government spokesman said.
"We know that Pakistan wants to sabotage every peace measure initiated by the Afghans themselves," spokesman Amrullah quoted Masood as telling the U.N. official.

The official Kabul radio said the Foreign Ministry issued a statement later repeating the charge and urging Pakistani President Farooq Leghari to stop the alleged interference "before the situation in the region becomes worse".

Taleban refuses to talk to Rabbani unless he steps down, and a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said on Saturday the militia had declined an Iranian invitation to attend a planned regional conference in Tehran to discuss ways to end the conflict because the Kabul government would be there.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted a Taleban spokesman in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar, Maulvi Abdul Wakil, as saying the militia leadership told an Iranian delegation that they would not attend any conference where Kabul's present "unrepresentative government" was represented.
Wakil said Taleban had also rejected Iran's offer to mediate between it and the Kabul government and told the delegation that Tehran was not impartial and was backing Rabbani.
The charge is denied by Iran, which has been planning to host a conference of foreign ministers of countries neighbouring Afghanistan in Tehran on October 29-30.

Goulding urged Taleban to show willingness to sit down and talk with other leaders about bringing the war to an end and said he would "repeat this policy of the United Nations" at a meeting with the militia in Kandahar early next week.

"Nobody is going to get everything they want, they should give up something and once we are satisfied that those conditions exist that there is a willingness as such then we will forward ideas as to how we think they might succeed in making their transition from the horrors that exist at present."
Goulding, who was accompanied by special U.N. envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl, said the Kabul government was supportive of the U.N. peace efforts.
He said he and Holl planned to present their recommendations to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
